addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).

- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

This file contains near term tasks with a short description
and reference links to more details.

Intro paragraphs in `## Todo` and `## Bugs` should begin every
line with 1 leading space so they don't match the `^\d+\. `
pattern that locates numbered entries; 2 or 3 spaces also work.

## In Progress

When a `## Todo` item is picked up, its text **moves** here
(never copied — one home per text). The picked-up task is a
`###` heading; a multi-cycle program adds one level — the
program is the `###` and its current stage a `####` (headings
give the current work durable anchors, which numbered Todo
entries can't). The problem overview is followed by the
"plan" — a bulleted list of the development "ladder". Each
rung is prepended with its commit reference — a literal
`[[N]]` placeholder until the commit is pushed, then
backfilled to a real file-local `[[n]]` ref (same pattern as
the chores As-built rungs):
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-0 blah (done)
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-1 blah blah (current)
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-2 blah blah blah
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y close-out and validation

### Refactor: typed jj facade → jj-lib in-process; end subprocess spawning

Version-control operations were ~30 hand-rolled `run("jj", …)`
spawns plus every mutation, with per-module private wrappers
and raw-git vestiges in init — stderr parsing instead of typed
errors, and jj's single-attempt index-lock acquisition (the
push `bookmark-set` lock race in [bugs.md](notes/bugs.md))
can't be retried where it fails. A multi-ladder program; the
staged plan, design detail, and the eight absorbed former
Todos live in

 Entries are in **strict priority rank** — #1 highest,
 descending. Reprioritize by moving an entry, then
 `vc-x1 fix-todo --no-dry-run TODO.md` to renumber.
 The numbers are positional rank, not stable IDs — to refer
 to a Todo, name it by its **title** (a greppable mention;
 a numbered list item has no anchor to link to), not its
 number. Long-tail entries

 [Prose Form in AGENTS.md](/AGENTS.md#prose-form); deeper
 detail goes in `notes/chores/chores-NN.md` design
 subsections (link via `[N]` ref).

1. **refactor: jj-lib migration.** Facade internals and
   mutations move in-process; see
   [the stage](notes/refactor-20260716.md#stage-jj-lib-migration).
   Next cycle (0.78.0) — **planned but not opened**; the
   2026-07-29 session ended mid-design. Resume here.
   - **Decision needed before the pickup**: does 0.78.0 take
     all three pieces below, or the first two, deferring
     mutations until there is a reason to accept the version
     coupling? The conversation ended on that question.
     - **Retry around the existing spawns** — catch the lock
       failure, back off, retry. Fixes bugs.md #1, which is
       the cycle's headline prize. Zero coupling. Ugly:
       stderr matching, the very thing this program exists to
       delete.
     - **jj-lib for non-snapshotting reads** — `jj log`
       templates become `Commit` accessors. Real cleanup, no
       op-store writes, no coupling.
     - **jj-lib for mutations** — typed errors and the end of
       spawning, and the only piece that puts our jj-lib in
       the position of writing ops beside an unknown set of
       user-installed jj binaries.
   - **The prize does not require the risk.** jj-lib does not
     *enable* the index-lock retry — it makes the retry's
     error handling typed rather than stringly. The retry can
     wrap the spawn today.
   - **The coexistence question is answered**, and the answer
     is "unenforceable, probably fine": see
     [the risk section](notes/refactor-20260716.md#design-risk-op-store-coexistence)
     for the evidence. Short form — structural change fails
     closed, the index self-heals, the op store has no
     version stamp so evolutionary change is undetectable, jj
     publishes no compatibility policy, and a `jj --version`
     gate is defeated by users having several jj binaries
     installed.
   - `@`-relative reads ("uncommitted changes right now?")
     need a working-copy snapshot, which is an op-store
     write — so they move with the mutations, not with the
     other reads.
   - Draft ladder, if all three: `-0` open the cycle; `-1`
     settle the version-coupling policy and record it; `-2`
     reads via jj-lib; `-3` mutations + the deferred `@`
     reads; `-4` index-lock retry (bugs.md #1) with a
     `git init --bare` → gix rider; close-out.

   `push` (decided 2026-07-28) — publishes a close-out as a
   non-fast-forward merge; body-intro validation rides as
   the first rung. See
   [trapezoid close-out](notes/refactor-20260716.md#stage-trapezoid-close-out)
   and
   [push body-intro validation](notes/refactor-20260716.md#stage-push-body-intro-validation).

 582  582: ## Design risk: op-store coexistence
 583  583: 
 584     : We think in-process op-store writes must coexist with the
 585     : user's external `jj` CLI driving the same repos; jj-lib 0.41

 589     : approach.
      584: In-process op-store writes must coexist with the user's
      585: external `jj` CLI driving the same repos. Investigated
      586: 2026-07-29 (jj-lib 0.41 source, installed jj 0.40.0, jj's
      587: published docs). Findings, and why the obvious mitigation
      588: does not work:
      589: 
      590: - **Today there is no risk at all.** vc-x1 spawns the user's
      591:   `jj` for every mutation, so it inherits their version. The
      592:   migration *introduces* the coupling; it does not inherit
      593:   one.
      594: - **Structural change fails closed.** `repo.rs:491-569` /
      595:   `workspace.rs:513` raise `StoreLoadError::UnsupportedType`
      596:   when a `type` file names a backend the library lacks — a
      597:   future `op_store/type` we don't know is a hard error, not a
      598:   guess.
      599: - **The index self-heals.** It carries an explicit format
      600:   version (`COMMIT_INDEX_SEGMENT_FILE_FORMAT_VERSION = 6`,
      601:   checked at `default_index/readonly.rs:303`), and
      602:   `default_index/store.rs:560` responds to a mismatch by
      603:   reindexing, not erroring. Derived data; costs time only.
      604:   Reading those bytes ourselves is inert — it does not
      605:   trigger the rebuild — but the constant is `pub(super)`, so
      606:   a check of our own would duplicate a private constant and
      607:   an internal file layout.
      608: - **The op store has no version stamp.** It serializes with
      609:   protobuf (`simple_op_store.rs:159-218`), whose evolution
      610:   rule is that unknown fields are skipped. So an evolutionary
      611:   change — same backend type, new fields — is *undetectable*
      612:   by construction: a reader cannot distinguish "field absent"
      613:   from "field present and unknown to me". The realistic

400:is reshaped between two pushes (the recipe below). For any
401:other shape, drive `jj git push` directly.
402:
403:### Trapezoid close-out recipe
404:
405:A [trapezoid](#shape-at-close-out-push) close-out is
406:published in four steps: an ordinary close-out push, a
407:two-command reshape, and a second push that re-points the
408:bookmark at the reshaped commit.
409:
410:```
411:  main line   …──<base>──────────────────<closeout>──
412:                    \                    /
413:  ladder             <rung-1>──…──<tip>─┘
414:```
415:
416:- `<base>` — the **parent of the ladder's first rung**, which
417:  is the trunk position when the cycle opened. It becomes the
418:  first parent.
419:- `<tip>` — the cycle's last Work commit. It becomes the
420:  second parent.
421:- `<closeout>` — the close-out commit, created by step 1.
422:
423:The steps. Only step 1 is a `vc-x1 push`; the rest is jj,
424:because after step 1 the commits already exist and all that
425:remains is reshaping and publishing them:
426:
427:1. `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --title "…" --body "…"`
428:   - the ordinary close-out push. It commits both repos, stamps the
429:   `ochid:` trailers, and publishes `<closeout>` linearly.
430:2. `jj rebase -r <closeout> --onto <base> --onto <tip>`
431:   - `<closeout>` becomes the merge. Parent order is the
432:   argument order.
433:3. `jj new <closeout>`
434:   -  puts an empty `@` above the merge.
435:4. `jj git push --bookmark <bookmark> -R .`
436:   - publishes the
437:   reshaped commit. The bookmark needs no `jj bookmark set`:
438:   it follows the rewrite in step 2 automatically. The bot
439:   repo is untouched, and its session tail goes out with a
440:   separate `vc-x1 squash-push` afterwards.
441:
442:**Step 4 is not a `vc-x1 push`** (corrected at the `0.77.0`
443:close-out, which tried it). Push runs its whole pipeline or
444:none of it, and the bot repo is never quiet for long: by the
445:time the reshape is done, `.claude` holds the session writes
446:from steps 1–3, so `commit-bot` wants to run and the message
447:stage demands a title for it. The result is a bot-side
448:requirement blocking a work-side publish that needs nothing
449:but a moved ref. Publishing an already-made commit is a
450:different operation from committing and publishing, and only
451:the latter is push's job.
452:
453:#### Details
454:
455:- **Verify two parents before step 4.** `jj log -r <closeout>
456:  -T 'parents.map(|p| p.change_id().short(8))'` must list
457:  both. jj preserves the second parent even though `<base>`
458:  is an ancestor of `<tip>` (observed at `0.74.0`, `0.75.0`,
459:  `0.76.0`), but a collapsed merge is indistinguishable from
460:  a correct one in `jj log --no-graph` and is only visible
461:  once published.
462:- **`<base>` is not always the previous close-out.** A docs
463:  or planning interlude between cycles sits on the trunk line
464:  and must stay there; take the parent of the ladder's first
465:  rung, not the last close-out.
466:- **Step 3 is about `@`, not the bookmark.** The bookmark
467:  follows the rewrite in step 2 on its own. What step 2
468:  leaves misplaced is the working copy: `jj rebase -r`
469:  re-parents descendants onto the rebased commit's **old**
470:  parent, so the empty `@` from step 1 lands beside the merge
471:  on `<tip>` — and the working tree reverts to pre-close-out
472:  content, which looks alarming and isn't. `jj new` puts `@`
473:  back on top of the merge so the tree is right and the next
474:  commit continues from there. Skipping it doesn't break the
475:  publish; it leaves you working from the wrong parent.
476:- **Trailers survive.** The reshape changes `<closeout>`'s
477:  SHA but not its change ID, so the `ochid:` trailers stamped
478:  in step 1 stay valid in both directions. This is why the
479:  reshape is safe after the trailers are written.
480:- **Step 4 moves the bookmark sideways.** Step 1's SHA
481:  becomes unreachable; anyone who fetched between the two
482:  pushes holds a dangling commit. Consequently a
483:  [`Commits:` backfill](#commits-backfill) must never read a
484:  SHA from that window — wait until step 4 lands.
485:- **Immutability.** No flag is needed on a long-lived topic
486:  bookmark. Only when `<closeout>` is already on `trunk()`
487:  does the rebase need `--ignore-immutable`, and then the
488:  push force-updates the target.
489:- **The bot repo is left for afterwards.** Step 4 touches only
490:  the work repo, so `.claude` still holds every session write
491:  from the whole procedure. `vc-x1 squash-push` folds that
492:  tail into the bot commit — its change id survives the
493:  squash, so the work-side `ochid:` keeps resolving.
494:
495:#### Recovery
496:
497:- **Nothing is published between steps 2 and 3** — the local
498:  reshape is undoable with `jj undo` / `jj op restore`.
499:- **A collapsed or mis-parented merge** (step 2 verification
500:  fails): undo and redo step 2 with the corrected revisions.

content.text:
I rendered your version through two parsers, and the numbering loss is an indent bug, not a trade-off you have to accept. Your nested bullets sit at **3 spaces**. CommonMark/GFM (what GitHub uses) accepts that and nests correctly — numbering survives. Strict-4-space parsers (python-markdown, and anything built on it) don't recognize the nesting and flatten the sub-bullets into the *same* ordered list, so your four steps render as eight numbered items: ```
  • cmd --body "x"
  • the desc. It commits both, stamps trailers.
    • ← became step 2
  • jj rebase
    • ← became step 3 ``` Indent the `-` to **4 spaces** (continuations to 6) and both parsers nest it properly and keep 1–4. Verified with `cmark-gfm` and python-markdown just now. Two smaller defects in the current text: step 3 has a double space after its `-`, and every continuation line is at 3 spaces, relying on lazy continuation rather than lining up under the bullet. One thing worth weighing before you settle: `` `cmd` — description `` is the pervasive shape in this file (lines 314–317, 638, 664, 670, 678–683) and in AGENTS.md, including other numbered step lists. The `--` confusion only actually bites when the command *ends* in an option or a value — steps 1 and 4 here, and `jj diff --from --to ` at line 316.

content.text:
Looked at it. I agree with the change, and I think the case for it is stronger than the two reasons you gave — but one of your two reasons doesn't hold up.

**The real win is that the marker becomes terminal.** On the em-dash rungs, the line carries five things at once: ref, version, title, status, and the opening clause of a paragraph. Because titles differ in length, `(done)` lands at a different column on every rung and has text running on after it, so it never forms a scannable column. In your -5 form the rung line *ends* at the marker. That's a much stronger visual cue than grep, and it's the thing that actually makes the ladder scan.

**The grep argument is weaker than you think.** Titles longer than ~50 chars wrap, and -5 is exactly that case: grepping `(done)` returns

```
  stretches` (done)
```

— no ref, no version, no full title. On -3 the marker at least shares a line with the version and title. So for wrapped titles the sub-bullet form makes grep slightly *worse*, not better. It's a wash overall; lead with the scanning argument instead.

**The convention already requires this — twice.** Prose Form says "avoid wall-of-prose paragraphs — they hide the structure that bullets make scannable," and the Semicolons-inside-bullets rule says a bullet joining clauses is "a list hiding inside running prose." The -3 lead is a nine-line paragraph containing a colon-list of three signals (drift / bursts / interference) plus two parenthetical asides — a list hiding in prose by any reading. -4, -6, -7 are the same shape. So this isn't a new rule for iiac-perf, it's applying an existing one to a surface that escaped it. That matters if you later want it to fan out to the template family.

**The principled framing:** the rung line is a *title* (ref + version + title + status = the rung's identity) and the sub-bullets are its *body*. That's the same split AGENTS.md already makes in Conventional-commit shape. The em-dash form blends identity and body into one run-on; the sub-bullet form makes the split structural instead of punctuational. Worth stating that way, because it answers the follow-up question cleanly: nothing but identity goes on the rung line.

Three things I'd weigh before committing to it:

- **Uniform, or only when there's bulk?** -1, -2 and -7 have lead prose but no existing sub-bullets, so converting them creates one-item sublists. A soft rule ("keep it on the line if it fits in one line") avoids that but drifts, and drift is how -3 grew to nine lines in the first place. I'd take the singletons — uniformity is what makes a scan-list scan, and -0 already shows the form degrading gracefully to a bare rung line.
- **Don't merge this with the cycle-protocol.md question.** Same fix, different root cause: there the driver was an em-dash sitting next to `--body "…"` and reading as an option; here it's prose bulk. If you write one rule covering both, state both reasons or it'll look arbitrary to a future reader.
- **Sub-bullet indent, if you render outside GitHub.** I tested iiac-perf's existing 2-space sub-bullets: `cmark-gfm` nests them correctly, but python-markdown (4-space rule) flattens them into siblings of the rung — the same failure you hit in cycle-protocol.md, and it's already present throughout that ladder, not something the change introduces. If your renderer is in that family, 4-space sub-bullets work in both. If you only ever read this on GitHub or in VS Code, it's moot.

One non-issue: `fix-todo` only touches `## Todo` and `## Bugs` (`src/fix_todo.rs:1-2, 66`), so `## In Progress` is entirely hand-maintained and no tooling will fight the restructure.

content.text:
Endorse the ban. The rule as drafted has one rationale that overreaches, one that's soft, a missing gap that covers a quarter of the real uses, and no migration policy. Here's the breakdown.

**The strongest reason isn't in the draft.** Em dashes are asymmetric: free for an LLM to emit, awkward for a human to type, grep, or scan. That asymmetry is *why* there are 2,514 of them across 39 files in vc-x1 — nobody chose them, they accumulated because the writer pays nothing and the reader pays every time. That's a much better argument than either one given, and it's the one that survives someone objecting "but I can read em dashes fine."

**"At terminal sizes it reads like `-` or `--`" overreaches.** In most monospace fonts `—` is visibly longer than `-`. What actually bit was contextual: `--body "…" — the ordinary…`, where the dash sits next to option syntax and your eye pattern-matches it as another flag. That's real but conditional. Stating it as universal invites a future reader to test it, find it false in their font, and discount the whole rule. Say the conditional version.

**"Can't be typed into a grep" is true but soft.** A validator scans bytes without caring, and `rg -e $'\u2014'` works. It's the human doing ad-hoc search who pays. Keep it, rank it second.

**The gap: no colon.** 615 of the 2,514 (about a quarter) are a bullet-title separator, and a large share of those are *definition lists*, not title-plus-body:

```
- `jj diff` — working-copy diff (uncommitted)
- `jj diff -r @-` — diff of the previous commit
- `<base>` — the parent of the ladder's first rung
```

Comma reads wrong there, parentheses invert the emphasis, two sentences is absurd, and sub-bullets turn four scannable lines into eight with one-item sublists. The answer is a colon, and the draft doesn't name it. Tell: the draft's own final sentence uses a colon for exactly this job — "sharing a line: make the body sub-bullets."

So the rule needs three cases, not one: prose dash → comma/parens/split (or delete — a lot of these join an aside that shouldn't be there); term-definition → colon; title-plus-body → sub-bullets.

**The two rationales imply different scopes, and neither matches the rule's text.** "Reads like `-`" covers `—` and `–` but not `…`. "Can't be typed" covers `—`, `–`, `…`, `→` — and these three files alone hold 26 ellipses and 22 arrows, all of which the rule silently permits. Pick the visual rationale (it's the one that motivated this), then say explicitly that `–` is in and `…`/`→` are out because they're unambiguous. Otherwise the first person to notice `…` reads the rule as arbitrary.

**Migration needs a sentence.** 2,514 sites in vc-x1, and these files fan out to the template family. About 75% are prose dashes where the replacement is a judgment call, so this isn't a `sed` — it's bot-hours. Without a stated policy you get a permanently mixed corpus and no way to tell "not yet converted" from "exception." The AGENTS.md precedent is the chores-conventions line: applies going forward, existing text keeps its form until touched.

**Keep it a hard ban.** AGENTS.md usually writes leans-with-a-why (the unwrap rule says "a lean, not a ban"), but that's because unwrap is sometimes the clearest code. There's no sentence that *needs* an em dash, and soft punctuation rules drift — drift is how you got 2,514. A hard ban is also the rare prose rule that's mechanically checkable, which is worth one line since `validate-repo` is already on the roadmap.

A redraft:

```
### No em dashes

Don't use `—` (or `–`). Adjacent to option syntax it reads as
another flag — `--body "…" — the` scans as three options — and
it can't be typed at a terminal, so it's invisible to ad-hoc
grep. The cost is asymmetric: free to write, paid on every
read, which is why it accumulates. `…` and `→` are fine; they
carry no such ambiguity.

Replace by case:

- **Prose aside** — comma, parentheses, or two sentences.
  Often the aside should just go.
- **Term and definition** (`jj diff`, `<base>`, a flag) —
  a colon. Keeps a glossary or command list one line per entry.
- **Bullet title and its body** — that's a heading and a
  paragraph sharing a line; make the body sub-bullets.

Applies going forward; existing text converts when touched.
Checkable by byte scan, unlike most prose rules.
```

(That draft uses two em dashes to quote the thing it bans, which reads as a joke but is the honest way to show the failure case. Worth restructuring if you want the file itself to pass its own validator — probably you do.)

## Prose form

Long-lived prose on this project follows one basic shape: a short intro
that explains the *why* or the high-level *what*, then a `-` bullet
list for the details. Wrap lines at ≤72 cols (bullet continuations
indent two spaces). Avoid wall-of-prose paragraphs — they hide the
structure that bullets make scannable.

Surfaces that use this shape:

- Module / function / struct / field doc comments in `.rs` files —
  see [Doc comments](#doc-comments-on-every-file-function-and-method).
- Commit message bodies (both work-repo and bot-repo). The
  ≤50-col title is the commit-specific add-on; see
  [Per-commit flow](notes/cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow).
- Chore descriptions in `notes/chores/chores-NN.md` — see
  [Chores section content](#chores-section-content--no-edit-list-git-is-the-record).
- Todo and Done entries in `TODO.md` when an entry needs more
  than one line of detail. Pure one-liners are still fine.

Bullet *content* differs by surface:

- **Commit bodies** — bullets are file-by-file: one bullet per file
  changed, file plus a one-line gist (e.g.
  `README.md: new Overview intro`). Source of truth for the
  mechanical edit list.
- **Chores / todo / done** — bullets are conceptual (design points,
  structural notes, the "what landed and why" at a notch above
  file-list granularity). Never a copy of the commit's edit list —
  see [Chores section content](#chores-section-content--no-edit-list-git-is-the-record).
- **Doc comments** — bullets are whatever structure fits (fields,
  cases, invariants).

### Problem + plan shape

`## In Progress` cycle blocks, chores section intros, and `## Todo`
entries use a sharper form of the same shape:

- **Problem statement** (the why) — one or two sentences;
  don't pad with intent, don't restate the plan.
- **Plan bullets** (the what/when) — formality differs by
  surface:
  - In Progress / chores: a committed ladder, one step per
    commit — see

Agreed, they belong together, and you've got the unifying idea right. Let me sharpen it and then argue for one structural refinement.

**The unification.** An em dash is punctuation for *not deciding*. It joins two things without naming their relationship, which is exactly what a wall-of-prose paragraph does at paragraph scale and what `A; B; C` does at clause scale. Prose form's thesis is already "make the structure explicit so it scans"; the em dash is that failure at its smallest unit. Under that framing the three replacements aren't three unrelated fixes, they're three answers to *what structure were you avoiding naming?* — sub-bullets, a colon, a full stop. That's one rule, and it's this section's rule.

**The refinement: siblings, not a merge.** You already have `### Semicolons inside bullets` doing precisely this job for `;`. The temptation is to fold both into one "punctuation that defers structure" section, but the members are lopsided — semicolons need four lines and a soft exception, em dashes need three cases, a scope statement, and a hardness justification. A merged section where one member is 6× the other reads as a rule with an appendix. Keep them as two `###` siblings and state the kinship once in the Prose form intro. That gets you the combination without the awkward shape.

Concretely, three edits.

**1. Prose form intro** — one sentence after line 282, which also fixes that sentence's own em dash:

```
Avoid wall-of-prose paragraphs: they hide the structure that
bullets make scannable. Punctuation that joins clauses without
naming their relationship is the same failure at sentence scale;
see [Semicolons inside bullets](#semicolons-inside-bullets) and
[No em dashes](#no-em-dashes).
```

**2. `### Semicolons inside bullets`** — unchanged except its own em dash on line 329 becomes a colon.

**3. New `### No em dashes`**, placed directly after it:

```
### No em dashes

Don't use `—` or `–` in durable text. Unlike the semicolon rule
above, this one is absolute, because the cost is asymmetric: an
em dash is free to emit and paid on every read, so it
accumulates without anyone having chosen it. Next to option
syntax the eye reads it as another flag, and it can't be typed
at a terminal, so it is invisible to ad-hoc grep. `…` and `→`
carry no such ambiguity and are fine.

An em dash usually stands in for a structural decision that was
not made. Make the decision:

- **A bullet's title and its body sharing a line** is a heading
  and a paragraph. Make the body sub-bullets.
- **A term and its definition** (`jj diff`, `<base>`, a flag)
  takes a colon, which keeps a glossary or a command list at
  one line per entry.
- **A prose aside** takes a comma, parentheses, or two
  sentences. Often the aside should just go.

Scope is durable text the bot writes (AGENTS.md, `notes/`,
commit bodies, chores sections), the same scope as
[Speculation marker](#speculation-marker). Applies going

code span is a specimen, not a use, the same way a `[N]` inside
backticks is not a citation. Unlike most prose rules this one

```

Two notes on why that scope line is doing real work: Prose form's own "Surfaces that use this shape" list covers doc comments, commit bodies, chores, and todo/done — it does *not* cover AGENTS.md or `notes/` prose generally. Without the explicit scope, the ban would inherit the narrower list and formally not apply to the file it's written in. Borrowing Speculation marker's scope fixes that and ties it to the existing durable-text rule, which is this rule's real structural twin.

**What this costs you immediately:** the Prose form section itself has about ten em dashes in 58 lines, and line 314 is a perfect specimen of both rules at once —

```

  don't pad with intent, don't restate the plan.
```

## Prose form

Long-lived prose on this project follows one basic shape: a short intro
that explains the *why* or the high-level *what*, then a `-` bullet
list for the details. Wrap lines at ≤72 cols (bullet continuations
indent two spaces). Avoid wall-of-prose paragraphs: they hide the
structure that bullets make scannable. Punctuation that joins
clauses without naming their relationship is the same failure at
sentence scale; see
[Semicolons inside bullets](#semicolons-inside-bullets) and
[No em dashes](#no-em-dashes).

Surfaces that use this shape:

- Module / function / struct / field doc comments in `.rs` files —
  see [Doc comments](#doc-comments-on-every-file-function-and-method).
- Commit message bodies (both work-repo and bot-repo). The
  ≤50-col title is the commit-specific add-on; see
  [Per-commit flow](notes/cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow).
- Chore descriptions in `notes/chores/chores-NN.md` — see
  [Chores section content](#chores-section-content--no-edit-list-git-is-the-record).
- Todo and Done entries in `TODO.md` when an entry needs more
  than one line of detail. Pure one-liners are still fine.

Bullet *content* differs by surface:
  - Todo entries: rough informal bullets, no numbering;
    formalized only when the entry is picked up into a
    cycle.

### Semicolons inside bullets

A bullet that joins multiple clauses with semicolons (`A; B; C`)
is a list hiding inside running prose: break the clauses into
sub-bullets so the structure shows. Semicolons in running prose
(intro paragraphs, sentence-joins) are fine. Not absolute: very
short clauses or tight pairs can stay joined inside a bullet when
breaking would be more noise than signal.

### No em dashes

Don't use `—` or `–` in durable text. Unlike the semicolon rule
above, this one is absolute, because the cost is asymmetric: an
em dash is free to emit and paid on every read, so it
accumulates without anyone having chosen it. Next to option
syntax the eye reads it as another flag, and it can't be typed
at a terminal, so it is invisible to ad-hoc grep. `…` and `→`
carry no such ambiguity and are fine.

An em dash usually stands in for a structural decision that was
not made. Make the decision:

- **A bullet's title and its body sharing a line** is a heading
  and a paragraph. Make the body sub-bullets.
- **A term and its definition** (`jj diff`, `<base>`, a flag)
  takes a colon, which keeps a glossary or a command list at
  one line per entry.
- **A prose aside** takes a comma, parentheses, or two
  sentences. Often the aside should just go.

Scope is durable text the bot writes (AGENTS.md, `notes/`,
commit bodies, chores sections), the same scope as
[Speculation marker](#speculation-marker). Applies going

code span is a specimen, not a use, the same way a `[N]` inside
backticks is not a citation. Unlike most prose rules this one
is checkable by byte scan, with code spans skipped.

**Accept: the reordering and the grammar fix.** Reasons first, verdict last reads better than my verdict-then-because. And "the eye reads *one* as another flag, *neither* can be typed, *both* are invisible" correctly handles the two characters the sentence names — mine said "an em dash… it" right after naming `—` and `–`. **Accept: collapsing the scope to a pointer.** My version spelled out the surface list *and* said "the same scope as Speculation marker," which is the duplication this file keeps warning about. Theirs can't drift when Speculation marker's scope changes. Take it.

**Not a tweak, a localization: the dropped examples.** `jj diff` and `<base>` are jj and cycle-protocol terms; they'd be wrong in iiac-perf, so dropping them there is correct. Keep them here. They're carrying the ambiguous part of the bullet, which is what counts as a "term" (a command, a placeholder, a flag), not what a definition is.

One sentence closes it, and it's the sentence that scopes the rule to *visual ambiguity with `-`* rather than to non-ASCII generally.

Without "applies going forward," every one of them is ambiguous — a reader at line 290 can't tell whether the rule is being violated or the sweep hasn't arrived. That's a live problem the moment this lands, not a hypothetical, and the file already has the precedent: the chores conventions end with "Any pre-existing sections… keep their free-form text; the convention applies going forward."

**Accept, with a caveat: cutting the byte-scan note.** It's an implementation note for a validator that doesn't exist, and it doesn't belong in a prose-style rule. ### No em dashes

Don't use `—` or `–` in durable text. Unlike the semicolon rule
above, this one is absolute, because the cost is asymmetric: an
em dash is free to emit and paid on every read, so it
accumulates without anyone having chosen it. Next to option
syntax the eye reads it as another flag, and it can't be typed
at a terminal, so it is invisible to ad-hoc grep. `...` and `->`
carry no such ambiguity and are fine.

An em dash usually stands in for a structural decision that was
not made. Make the decision:

- **A bullet's title and its body sharing a line** is a heading
  and a paragraph. Make the body sub-bullets.
- **A term and its definition** (`jj diff`, `<base>`, a flag)
  takes a colon, which keeps a glossary or a command list at
  one line per entry.
- **A prose aside** takes a comma, parentheses, or two
  sentences. Often the aside should just go.

Scope is durable text the bot writes (AGENTS.md, `notes/`,
commit bodies, chores sections), the same scope as
[Speculation marker](#speculation-marker). Applies going
forward; existing text converts when touched. A `—` inside a
code span is a specimen, not a use, the same way a `[N]` inside
backticks is not a citation. Unlike most prose rules this one
is checkable by byte scan, with code spans skipped.

Done. Both files are clean, and the only `…` / `→` left in AGENTS.md are the two specimen lines inside the rule itself (342, 349).

**What changed**

- **Bulk replacement** in `AGENTS.md` and `notes/cycle-protocol.md`: 13 + 8 ellipses → `...`, 10 + 2 arrows → `->`.
- **Rule rewritten and renamed** to `### Typeable punctuation only` (`AGENTS.md:339`), now banning `—`, `–`, `…`, `→` on the single rationale you gave: none can be typed at a terminal, so none can be grepped. The em dash keeps its extra reason (reads as a flag next to option syntax) and keeps the three structural replacements, since it's the only one without a mechanical substitute.
- **Prose form intro link** updated to the new anchor.
- I also folded in the iiac-perf review while I was in the paragraph: their reordering and the collapsed scope pointer, my migration-policy sentence. The `…`/`→` carve-out I'd argued for is gone, since you've banned them instead — that resolves the inconsistency I flagged in the cleaner direction.

**Three things worth knowing**

- **The rename was forced.** "No em dashes" is wrong for a rule covering four characters. If you'd rather keep a concrete heading, `### No em dashes, ellipses, or arrows` works and only the one link at line 286 needs following.
- **The ASCII diagram needed a manual fix.** `notes/cycle-protocol.md:410-412` is aligned art, and `…` → `...` shifted `<base>` two columns right. I re-indented the `\` / `/` line by two to restore the exact original geometry. Note the diagram still uses `──` and `┘` box-drawing, which are equally untypeable — I left them since they're art, not punctuation, but the rule as written doesn't carve them out.
- **The two files are now out of step with the rest of the repo.** `README.md:1264`, `notes/README.md:56`, `notes/done.md:62`, and `notes/chores/chores-04.md` (5 sites) all still write `// OK: …`, which no longer matches the `### \`// OK: ...\` comments on \`unwrap*\` calls` heading in AGENTS.md. That heading is only referenced as plain text, not as an anchor link, so nothing is broken — but the convention's name now has two spellings in the corpus.

Also still outstanding from the earlier review: the byte-scan validator note I dropped from the rule should land as a `validate-repo` TODO entry, including that code spans must be skipped or the check flags its own line 342. Want me to add it?

content.text:
Only one substantive change: the scope paragraph. (The other diff hunk is an iiac-perf-local convention about the version-of-record bullet leading a commit body — unrelated to this rule.)

**Accept it. They caught a real bug in my text, and it's one my own edits already disproved.**

My version said "A banned character inside a code span is a specimen, not a use" — a blanket code-span exemption. But look at what I actually converted an hour ago: `` `.expect(…)` `` → `` `.expect(...)` ``, `` `#[arg(…)]` `` → `` `#[arg(...)]` ``, `` `--title "…"` `` → `` `--title "..."` ``. Every one of those is inside a code span. The majority of the ellipsis sites in AGENTS.md were. So my rule as written forbade the sweep I had just performed. Their "exempt only when it is naming the character itself" fixes exactly that, and the `.expect` example is the right one to lead with because it's the case that breaks the naive reading.

Their grammar fix is right too. Mine had a comma splice ("applies going forward, existing text converts when touched"); splitting into two sentences with the semicolon inside the second is correct.

**One gap to add: verbatim quotation.**

Their rule sorts code spans into two bins — naming the character (exempt) and doing a job (converts). There's a third: **quoting text that isn't ours**, where converting silently falsifies a record.

This isn't hypothetical here. 27 of the last 400 commit titles in this repo contain a banned character:

```
docs: process observation → chores (0.62.0-10)
docs: move ## Bugs → notes/bugs.md (0.58.0-2)
refactor: bm_track → debug! (0.52.0-1)
```

Those are pushed and immutable. And AGENTS.md's own Conventional-commit shape rule requires the chores `##` header, the `## Done` entry, and the commit title to be **identical** — so under their rule as written, converting a quoted title to `->` breaks that identity and breaks `git log --grep "<title>"`. Same for quoted tool output and error messages.

Suggested addition, one sentence onto their paragraph:

```
Text quoted verbatim from outside this repo's prose (tool
output, an error message, a pushed commit title) keeps its
characters: converting it would falsify the quote and break
`git log --grep`.
```

**One state note, not a criticism:** iiac-perf's AGENTS.md still holds 15 ellipses, 11 arrows, and 114 em dashes, so it states a rule its own text violates ~140 times. That's exactly what "applies going forward, existing text converts when touched" licenses, and vc-x1 is in the same position on em dashes (117). Worth being deliberate that this is the intended state rather than an oversight.

Want me to apply their paragraph plus the quotation clause here?

## Speculation marker

Durable text the bot writes — AGENTS.md, `notes/`, commit bodies,
chores sections — should stick to observations and direct descriptions
of the code or data. If a mechanism, hypothesis, or causal claim
enters the text, prefix it with "We think ..." (a royal "we") so a
reader can tell the measured from the inferred.

**Why:** unmarked speculation reads like evidence, and a future reader
(or the bot on a later session) can pick it up as a known fact when
it's not. Measured / inferred is a distinction worth keeping visible
in the written record.

content.text:
Their rewrite is better than mine on every point, and one of the changes catches a hole neither of us had seen.

**"is transcribed, not written" is the right justification.** Mine argued from consequence ("converting would falsify the quote"); theirs states the principle — the ban governs authoring, and transcription isn't authoring. That generalizes for free to filenames, URLs, pasted config, anything quoted, without enumerating them. Mine would have needed a new clause per case.

**"this overrides the code-span rule above" fixes a real conflict in my version.** Their code-span rule says a banned character "doing a job inside a code span is a use, and converts." A quoted commit title in a code span *is* doing a job, so my paragraph and that one contradicted each other and mine didn't say which won. Theirs does.

**"Titles written from here on comply" closes a self-perpetuating loophole.** Without it, "quoted titles keep their characters" licenses writing a *new* title with an arrow, after which every chores header and `## Done` entry quoting it is permanently exempt. Sharp catch.

**"already-published" beats my "pushed"** — states the property that makes it immutable rather than the jj operation that got it there.

Two things left.

**1. The scope inherits "commit bodies," not titles — so that last sentence is load-bearing and misplaced.** Speculation marker's scope is "AGENTS.md, `notes/`, commit bodies, chores sections." Commit *titles* are formally outside it, which means "Titles written from here on comply" is the only sentence putting them in scope at all, and it's sitting at the tail of a paragraph about quotation exemptions. A reader asking "may I use an arrow in a commit title?" won't look there.

Fix it at the scope line instead, which also lets the sentence go:

```
Scope is the same as [Speculation marker](#speculation-marker),
plus commit titles. It applies going forward; existing text
converts when touched.
```

Don't amend Speculation marker itself — a ≤50-col title has no room for "We think," so its exclusion of titles is probably deliberate.

**2. The exemption needs to apply outside code spans too.** "This overrides the code-span rule above" can be read as scoping the exemption *to* code spans. But the most common quoted-title site is a chores `##` header, and this file's own convention is that "the `##` header *is* the bare title" — bare prose, no backticks. Four words fix it:

```
transcribed, not written, so it keeps its characters, whether
or not it sits in a code span. This overrides the code-span
rule above.
```

Non-issue: line 364 at 78 cols is the anchor link, same width as the file's two other uses of it.

Net effect of both edits is one line shorter than what they have now. `./AGENTS-iiac-perf.md` still holds my weaker version — want me to sync it to theirs and apply these two, so the copy is the current candidate?

1	# AGENTS.md - Bot Instructions
2	
3	## Project Structure
4	
5	This project uses **two separate jj-git repos**:
6	
7	1. **Work repo** (`/` — project root): the project's generated
8	   artifact — code, prose, image, song, whatever it produces.
9	2. **Bot repo** (`/.claude/`): Contains Claude Code session data.
10	
11	Both repos are managed with `jj` (Jujutsu), which coexists with git.
12	
13	**Terminology.** "Work repo" and "bot repo" are the standard
14	names; write them as two words, adding a hyphen only when the
15	pair sits directly in front of another noun ("work-repo
16	commit", "bot-repo side"). Notes:
17	
18	- `.claude` is the bot repo's *path*, not its name — commands
19	  (`-R .claude`) and ochid paths (`/.claude/<chid>`) keep the
20	  literal path.
21	- The vc-x1 CLI's scope name for the work repo is `code`
22	  (`--scope=code|bot|code,bot`).
23	- "Work commit" / "Work-N" (capitalized) is a cycle-stage term
24	  (see [Cycle Protocol](#cycle-protocol)), not a repo name; a
25	  generic commit landing in the work repo is a "work-repo
26	  commit", never a bare "work commit".
27	
28	**Committing vs pushing.** Default to `vc-x1 push` — it commits and
29	publishes both repos together, each carrying one `ochid:` pointing at
30	the other (see [Cycle Protocol](#cycle-protocol) and
31	[ochid trailers](#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)). Use a bare
32	`jj commit` (see [jj Basics](#jj-basics)) only when:
33	
34	- the change will never be published — no `ochid:`;
35	- the commit will be squashed away before its series is pushed
36	  (loop-and-squash) — no `ochid:`; it disappears in the squash;
37	- the commit will be pushed later as a non-top commit — `jj commit`
38	  and add its `ochid:` now, because `vc-x1 push` stamps only the
39	  topmost commit it pushes, never the ancestors.
40	
41	**What "commit" and "push" mean.** In an instruction, "commit",
42	"push", and "commit + push" all mean `vc-x1 push` — land *and*
43	publish — unless stated otherwise. A bare `jj commit` is asked for
44	by name: "local commit", "save locally", "just `jj commit`" (the
45	cases above). So the spoken default is publish; the local-only
46	save is the named exception. The approval around a push —
47	interactive by default, waived only by an explicit scoped
48	delegation — is the cycle protocol's
49	[Pushing policy](notes/cycle-protocol.md#policy).
50	
51	## Repo Paths (relative from project root)
52	
53	- Work repo: `.` (project root)
54	- Bot repo: `.claude`
55	  (symlink from `~/.claude/projects/<path-to-project-root>/.claude`)
56	
57	## Working Directory
58	
59	Prefer staying in the project root. Use `-R` flags or absolute paths
60	to target other directories rather than `cd`. If `cd` seems necessary,
61	discuss with the user first — losing track of cwd causes subtle
62	command failures downstream.
63	
64	When invoking shell commands, prefer the shortest unambiguous path —
65	usually relative to cwd (`ls notes/`, not
66	`ls /home/wink/data/prgs/rust/vc-x1/notes/`). Long absolute paths
67	clutter the transcript without adding information. Out-of-workspace
68	paths (`/tmp/...`, `~/.config/...`) stay absolute. Read/Edit/Write
69	tool args also stay absolute — that's a tool-boundary constraint,
70	not a stylistic choice.
71	
72	Run **one command per shell invocation** — don't bundle several
73	steps into a single compound script (`a && b; c`). Bundling hides
74	which step produced which output and makes a failure ambiguous;
75	executing one at a time keeps the details visible and reviewable.
76	Exceptions are a genuine pipeline (`grep | sort`) or a tight,
77	inseparable pair where the join is the point.
78	
79	## File reads — read the slice you need
80	
81	Long notes files are appended to over time. Read only the
82	slice your task needs; grep or read further on demand.
83	
84	- **`TODO.md`** (the routine acquaint read) — first
85	  ~60 lines covers intro + `## In Progress` + the top of the
86	  ranked `## Todo` (priorities, #1 highest). `Read` with
87	  `offset=0, limit=60`. `## Ideas` sits below `## Todo`; read

94	- **`notes/bugs.md`** — the bug list. Small; read whole
95	  when triaging a bug or chasing the `## Bugs` pointer in
96	  TODO.md.
97	- **`notes/done.md`** + **`notes/chores/chores-NN.md`** —
98	  historical / append-mostly. Scan headings first
99	  (`grep '^## ' notes/chores/chores-NN.md`), then read only
100	  the section you need.
101	
102	**Why:** the routine read should stay small. `TODO.md`
103	grows every cycle, so the backlog and bugs live in files
104	under `notes/` rather than inline; the same "slice you
105	need" rule applies to historical files.
106	
107	## Memory
108	
109	Do not use the bot's per-project memory directory
110	(`~/.claude/projects/<path>/memory/`). In a dual-repo setup with
111	AGENTS.md it provides no capability AGENTS.md doesn't already cover,
112	and it loses on discoverability:
113	
114	- **AGENTS.md** — at the repo root, a well-known location for bot
115	  instructions, committed, reviewable, visible to every collaborator
116	  (human or bot).
117	- **Memory directory** — hidden under the user's home, tied to one
118	  machine, invisible to anyone but the bot, never diffed or reviewed.
119	
120	Easy for everyone to find beats convenient for the bot alone. Put

122	
123	## Model delegation
124	
125	When spawning subagents, match the model to the task: use a
126	lesser model (e.g. Haiku or Sonnet) for mechanical or simple

142	**Why:** the technical form is precise but easy to misread;
143	the plain form catches misunderstandings early, when they are

content.text:
No. I was too quick last turn, and re-reading the two paragraphs together there's a real hole.

The preceding paragraph says:

> A code span is exempt **only** when it is naming the character itself.

That "only" is exhaustive language — it claims the naming case is the *sole* exemption inside code spans. The quotation paragraph then adds a second one ("keeps its characters, whether or not it sits in a code span"). For a quoted commit title in backticks, the two rules produce opposite answers, and "only" has a fair claim to winning, because exhaustive phrasing normally reads as deliberate rather than sloppy.

So "This overrides the code-span rule above" wasn't purely redundant. It was doing the work of resolving that conflict, and "whether or not it sits in a code span" doesn't fully replace it — it asserts the exemption but doesn't say it beats an exemption list that called itself closed. The reader most likely to trip on this is a bot applying the rules mechanically, which is the main reader.

**But restoring that sentence is the wrong fix.** It patches the symptom. The cause is that "only" makes a promise the section then breaks. Soften it and the conflict never arises:

```
Scope is the same as [Speculation marker](#speculation-marker),
plus commit titles. It applies going forward; existing text
converts when touched. A code span is not exempt in itself:
naming the character is a specimen and stays, which is how this
section names them; a banned character doing a job is a use and
converts, so `` `.expect(…)` `` becomes `` `.expect(...)` ``.
```

That states the actual principle — code-span-ness isn't what decides, the character's *role* is — and leaves room for transcription as a third role. Same line count as what's there now.

**With that change, I accept their "Text quoted" paragraph verbatim.** It needs nothing: "transcribed, not written" names the third role, and "whether or not it sits in a code span" is then a clarification rather than a contradiction. Their deletion was correct *given* the preceding paragraph gets fixed; it just shouldn't land on its own.

As the two paragraphs stand in iiac-perf right now, there's a hole. Want me to apply the "only" fix to the candidate?

content.content:
### Typeable punctuation only

Durable text uses punctuation that can be typed at a terminal.
Banned: `—`, `–`, `…`, `→`. None can be entered without a
compose key or a paste, so none can be grepped for, and an em
dash next to option syntax reads as another flag. Unlike the
semicolon rule above this one is absolute: they cost nothing to
write and are paid on every read, so a soft rule accumulates
them.

`…` becomes `...` and `→` becomes `->`. The dashes have no
single replacement, because an em dash usually stands in for a
structural decision that was not made. Make the decision:

- **A bullet's title and its body sharing a line** is a heading
  and a paragraph. Make the body sub-bullets.
- **A term and its definition** (`jj diff`, `<base>`, a flag)
  takes a colon, which keeps a glossary or a command list at
  one line per entry.
- **A prose aside** takes a comma, parentheses, or two
  sentences. Often the aside should just go.

Scope is the same as [Speculation marker](#speculation-marker),
plus commit titles. It applies going forward; existing text

# Versioning

How this project versions its commits and the running
artifact. The scheme — the cycle step-numbering and the
unique-per-commit aim — is generic and shared across projects:
this file is copied **verbatim**, with
[Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record)
covering each medium by conditional rather than per-project
edits.

## Terms

Three names, used as defined here across
[AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md),
[cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md), and the notes files:

- **version** — the per-commit version (e.g. `0.3.0-5.3.0`),
  written with `-` in prose, ladders, chores, todo, and commit
  talk; its suffix encodes the cycle phase (see
  [Step numbering](#step-numbering)).
- **version-of-record** — the authoritative stored copy of the
  version, in the project's manifest (see

## Step numbering

The cycle (Preparation -> Work -> Close-out; see
[cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md)) encodes each commit's
phase in the version suffix — the **final identifier `0` marks
a Preparation**:

- `X.Y.Z-0` — Preparation
- `X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, … — Work commits
- `X.Y.Z` — Close-out (bare version, no suffix)

**Preparation is optional.** A lightweight cycle — no ladder,
no setup commit — skips `-0` and starts at `-1` (its first
Work commit). The same holds at every level: a sub-cycle
needing no Preparation omits its `.0` (see Nesting). One that
grows a Preparation later adds the `0` step without
renumbering siblings.

Disambiguation:

- `-10` — Work commit #10 (final identifier `10`), not a
  Preparation.
- `-1.0` — Preparation of the `-1` sub-cycle (final
  identifier `0`).

**Nesting.** Sub-cycles append another level, recursively:

- `X.Y.Z-3.0` — Preparation of the `-3` sub-cycle
- `X.Y.Z-3.1`, `X.Y.Z-3.2` — its Work
- `X.Y.Z-3` — its Close-out
- `X.Y.Z-3.1.0` — Preparation of the `-3.1` sub-sub-cycle

Bump the version-of-record at the start of each phase, so the
active phase is recorded — and, per the preference above,
every commit carries a distinct version.

## refactor: stateless push

Picked up 2026-07-28. `push.rs` (~1.5k lines) holds the
`Stage` machine, TOML state persistence, eight stage bodies,
two sanity verifiers, and the interactive gates in one file.
The state file is where the defects come from: bugs.md #3 —
the rollback rewinds the *repos* but not the *state*, so the
rerun skipped the commit stages and republished a previous bot
commit — and both sanity verifiers exist largely to defend
against that staleness. Retiring it, deriving the resume point
from repo reality as standalone `squash-push` already does,
deletes the class rather than patching it. Fifth cycle of the
refactor program; see

content.text:
No good reason. You're right — I defaulted to a ladder because the protocol has one, not because this change needs one.

Per-file rungs buy nothing here. Nothing in `README.md` informs the edit in `AGENTS.md`; there's no dependency, no build, no test, so no bisect value. Splitting the rule from the sweep is worse than not splitting: it lands a rule nobody follows yet, then five commits citing a rule from a previous commit. And the cost is real — eight approval gates, eight commit messages, eight chores rungs, eight ochid stampings, plus splitting a working copy that's already written.

versioning.md sanctions the alternative outright: "A lightweight cycle — no ladder, no setup commit — skips `-0`."

**One commit, bare `0.77.1`.** That changes three things I just wrote:

- `Cargo.toml` / `Cargo.lock` → `0.77.1`, not `0.77.1-0`
- The `TODO.md` block moves out of `## In Progress` and becomes a `## Done` entry — work that never spans commits was never in progress
- The `chores-15.md` section stays as-is; it's the design record and it's already written to close-out shape

## docs: jj-lib design notes + trapezoid recipe

Commits:

A trunk-line interlude between `0.77.0` and the punctuation
cycle, carrying two threads from the 2026-07-29 session plus
the corrections the `0.77.0` close-out earned by attempting
the trapezoid recipe as written.

- The op-store coexistence risk was a stub asking for a spike;
  it is now answered, and the answer is "unenforceable,
  probably fine". Read out of jj-lib 0.41 source against an
  installed jj 0.40.0: structural change fails closed, the
  index self-heals by reindexing, the op store serializes with
  protobuf and carries no version stamp, and jj publishes no
  on-disk compatibility policy. We think the residual risk is
  low-probability, silent, and low-blast-radius.
- The mitigation that looked obvious does not work. A
  `jj --version` gate samples what `$PATH` resolves to, which
  says nothing about the jj an editor integration or a later
  session runs against the same repo. This workspace already
  has two.
- Consequence for the ladder: taking the coupling is a
  decision, not a step 0.78.0 can assume. The index-lock prize
  (bugs.md #1) does not require it, since a retry can wrap the
  existing spawn today.
- The trapezoid recipe's step 4 is `jj git push`, not
  `vc-x1 push`. Push runs its whole pipeline or none of it,
  and the bot repo is never quiet: by the time the reshape is
  done, `.claude` holds the session writes from steps 1-3, so
  `commit-bot` wants a title for a work-side publish that
  needs nothing but a moved ref.
